newsitem.title: USA: W.W. Grainger expenses should decline - analysts.
newsitem.headline: W.W. Grainger expenses should decline - analysts.

text.p: W.W. Grainger Inc, whose shares tumbled in the wake of disappointing 1997 first-quarter earnings, should see its expenses decline later in the year, industry analysts said Friday.

"The problem as I see it was in the (higher) warehousing, marketing and integration expenses," William Fiala, an analyst at Edward Jones, said of the quarter. "We should be seeing a peak in that expense line now."
Earlier Friday, Grainger reported first-quarter earnings of $1.03 a share, up from $0.98 a year ago.
The figure was below the First Call analysts' mean estimate of $1.08 and at the low end of the range of broker estimates of $1.03 to $1.11, sparking a sell-off.
Grainger shares fell more than five early Friday to a low of 70-1/2. The shares recovered to 73-3/8, off 2-7/8, in afternoon trading.

Bill Chapman, investor relations manager at Grainger, said the company's first-quarter results were the first to include Acklands, a Canadian industrial distribution business Grainger acquired in December.
"Acklands is not being integrated into our core operation. It will be run as a separate business unit," Chapman said.
"All that we have said is that we anticipate Acklands to be break-even to $0.05 a share dilutive effect in 1997."
Chapman declined to comment on the stock activity.
Analyst Fiala said there was disappointment on the level of spending for warehouse expenses, which climbed to $261.3 million from $216.5 million in the first quarter of 1996.
"(Grainger) also spent a lot on their computer systems in the wake of the Acklands purchase," Fiala said, adding that he expects those expenses to decline in future quarters.
Chapman said Grainger is taking steps to grow Ackland's business, although no exact timetable has been determined.

"We are investing in a product line expansion, we're considering adding branches in Eastern Canada and enhancing the logistics and information systems," Chapman said. "This will be a long-term proposition."
John Dempsey, an analyst at Barrington Research, said acquisition costs can often be higher than analysts and companies expect, affecting the results in the initial quarter after a merger closes.
"I believe (Grainger) will have it figured out by the second half," he said, commenting on the potential lasting effects of the Ackland's purchase.
